profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for the next two-week sprint of an internal research prototype that detects requirements smells in natural-language specifications using deep learning. The team has already trained early models on a manually labeled dataset, but the latest experiments show overfitting and poor performance on underrepresented smell categories. The meeting is between the ML engineer responsible for training and evaluation and the requirements engineering lead coordinating annotation and demo preparation. Their agenda is to decide how to expand the dataset, what exactly needs to be labeled next, how the next training/evaluation cycle will be run, and what must be delivered for an internal demo to the architecture review group. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for annotation scope, model retraining, ownership, and timeline for the next sprint.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: NLP model training, evaluation design, transfer learning, experiment reproducibility
members.background: Elena joined from a document intelligence startup and now works on research prototypes for developer tooling; she has been running the current requirements-smell experiments and maintaining the training pipeline.
members.private_state: She wants the next sprint to produce a defensible improvement over the current baseline without contaminating evaluation, because she expects the internal research committee to scrutinize methodology more than the demo polish.
hidden_assumptions: A 'gold set' is a strictly adjudicated holdout set that should not be reused for iterative tuning or demo-driven adjustments.
Keeping the 'same split' means preserving the exact previous document-level partition so results remain directly comparable and leakage is avoided.
Adding examples for the 'weak classes' primarily means collecting more positive instances for underrepresented smell labels, not spending annotation time on additional negatives.
A model is 'demo-ready' once it beats the current baseline on held-out evaluation and can run the end-to-end inference pipeline reliably, even if the presentation layer is basic.

members.name: Marcus Alvarez
members.expertise: Requirements quality, annotation guideline design, ISO 29148 interpretation, stakeholder-facing tooling
members.background: Marcus previously led requirements audits in a regulated enterprise environment and now oversees annotation quality and how the prototype will be shown to internal reviewers and domain experts.
members.private_state: He wants the next sprint to yield a convincing reviewer experience and cleaner annotations, because he needs the architecture review group to believe the prototype is practical enough to justify more domain data access.
hidden_assumptions: A 'gold set' is the cleaned, reviewer-trusted subset of examples that can be used both for quick validation and for showing realistic outputs in demos.
Keeping the 'same split' means preserving roughly the same train/validation/test proportions after newly labeled documents are added, not preserving identical document IDs.
Working on the 'weak classes' includes labeling full requirement documents so positive examples come with realistic surrounding negatives and context.
A system is 'demo-ready' once the dashboard highlights plausible smells on representative requirements packets in a way reviewers find credible, even if the offline metrics are still unstable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using or refreshing the 'gold set' before the next training cycle and demo.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means a protected adjudicated holdout reserved for final evaluation and error analysis, not something that should be updated for convenience or reused during iteration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means the cleaned high-trust subset that annotators have recently reviewed and that can be updated, reused for spot checks, and shown in the internal demo.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both communities commonly use the term 'gold set' positively and with an aura of quality, so the phrase signals shared rigor even though one treats it as immutable evaluation data and the other as a refreshed trusted sample.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the same split
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to keep the 'same split as last round' so comparisons stay fair.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means reusing the exact previous document-level train/validation/test partition IDs to avoid near-duplicate leakage across requirements from the same source documents.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means maintaining the same approximate 70/15/15 ratio after the new annotation batch is added, even if the documents are reshuffled.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'same split' sounds like a routine housekeeping detail rather than a decision point, and each person assumes their interpretation is the obvious standard way to preserve comparability.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the next sprint should 'add examples for the weak classes.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena expects targeted collection of additional positive examples for underrepresented smell labels such as optionality and comparative phrases, enough to reduce class imbalance efficiently.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus expects annotators to work through complete requirement packets containing those smells, which includes labeling many surrounding non-smell sentences to preserve context and annotation consistency.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the planning level, 'add examples' feels naturally aligned, and neither person thinks to spell out whether examples means only new positives or full-document annotation units with implicit negatives.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the goal is to have something 'demo-ready' by next Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means a reproducible model run that improves on the current baseline on the held-out evaluation set and can generate stable offline predictions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means the review dashboard can surface believable smell highlights on a curated packet of requirements, even if the measured improvement is modest or not yet final.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Demo readiness is a socially overloaded phrase in software teams, and because both are cooperative and under time pressure, each silently projects their own standard onto the same deadline language.

turns.inner_thought: The last run is clearly overfitting, and if we stumble into leakage or tune against the holdout again, the research committee will tear it apart. For me, next Friday only counts if I can show a reproducible gain over baseline on the protected evaluation set and the pipeline runs end to end without surprises. The UI can be rough as long as the methodology is clean.
turns.utterance: I think we should frame this sprint around two things: getting the overfitting back under control and making sure we have something demo-ready by next Friday. If we can tighten the data side and do one disciplined training cycle, we should be in a much better place.

turns.inner_thought: What I need is a reviewer experience that feels credible. The architecture group is not going to care about a tiny metric bump if the outputs look messy or the labels look inconsistent. So the priorities are to refresh the gold set so it reflects the cleaned annotations, add examples for the weak classes through realistic packets, and make sure Friday's materials show believable smell highlights.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, the main planning items are refreshing the gold set, adding examples for the weak classes, and getting a credible reviewer packet together for the group on Friday.

turns.inner_thought: As long as we reuse the exact prior document-level partition, I can compare directly to the current baseline and avoid cross-document contamination. If they reshuffle anything, the whole comparison gets muddy fast, especially with related requirements living in the same source docs.
turns.utterance: Yep. On the training side, I can turn a new run around pretty quickly as long as we keep the same split as last round so the comparison to the current baseline stays clean.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we'll preserve the same overall proportions after we import the new packet. I also want annotators to revisit the gold set because some of those trusted examples need a cleanup pass before we show them or use them for quick checks. And if we're targeting optionality and comparative phrases, the right way is to have the team work through the next packet fully so the positives sit in proper context.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I can have the annotators relabel the gold set and then work through the next packet to add more examples for optionality and comparative phrases.

turns.inner_thought: If I can get roughly forty additional positives across the weak labels, that's enough to justify another transfer-learning pass without dragging annotation into a giant effort. I just need enough signal to test whether the underrepresented classes improve. Then I can do one new readout on the holdout and see if the gain is real.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. Roughly forty more examples in the weak classes should be enough for me to do another transfer-learning run and get a fresh readout on the gold set.

turns.inner_thought: Forty documents' worth of additions is doable if we keep the packets intact. I don't want the team cherry-picking isolated lines because that usually hurts consistency and makes the reviewer story look artificial. Once those are imported, we'll just keep the same split in the usual sense by maintaining the ratio across train, validation, and test.
turns.utterance: That number should be manageable. We'll label full requirement documents so the context stays intact, and after import we'll keep the same split as last round.

turns.inner_thought: I need the adjudicated holdout frozen by Thursday, not drifting any later, or I can't lock the run and prepare a defensible analysis. Once that's in, I can stop training, generate stable predictions, and package the error analysis. That's what makes it demo-ready for me.
turns.utterance: Great. I really just need the updated gold set in hand by Thursday so I can freeze training and produce the demo-ready model, plus some error analysis for Friday.

turns.inner_thought: Thursday is fine because what matters most is that the dashboard shows believable highlights on the packet we've chosen for the reviewers. If those examples look sensible and the annotations feel clean, the group will see practical value even if the offline numbers are still settling.
turns.utterance: That timing works for me. What I mainly need by Friday's session is for the dashboard to show believable smell highlights on the reviewer packet.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, so once their new labels arrive, I'll merge in the added positives, leave the original partition IDs untouched, retrain, and compare against the prior baseline. If the holdout gain is there, we're in good shape. I should restate comparability so nobody changes the split bookkeeping on import.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Then I'll retrain as soon as the refreshed data lands and reuse the previous split setup so the comparison stays apples to apples.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned: annotation starts with the weak classes, using the next packet, and I'll send over the cleaned trusted subset once review is done. That should give Elena something current to validate against and give me demo material the reviewers will trust.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. We'll focus annotation on the weak classes first, and I'll send the cleaned gold set over as soon as the packet review is finished.
